title: The Price of Being Seen
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 23 of 40
content:
The newspaper photograph caught Greg in the middle of laughing and me in the middle of looking at him.

It should have been sweet. Instead the caption described me as the person who had finally settled Beach City's most eligible wandering musician, which was a remarkable number of assumptions to pack into fourteen words.

"Most eligible?" Greg said. "I wish somebody had told me."

"That's the part you're worried about?"

"No. That's the part I can joke about without sweating through my shirt."

We stood beside the laundromat's humming washers, reading the little local paper above a rack of detergent. The article was about a neighborhood music night. We'd helped set up microphones and stayed late to stack chairs. Somehow the reporter had decided the important story was my relationship status.

A customer behind us wanted to know whether the next concert would be free. Greg answered her politely and promised to check the community schedule. Then we took the paper to the editor's office two doors down.

She looked exhausted. Ink marked the side of her thumb; a stack of late notices had eaten half her desk.

"I'm glad you liked the picture," she began.

"We didn't come about the picture," I said.

Her smile faltered. "The caption?"

"It says I settled him. I didn't. We chose to spend time together. And there are other people in my life who didn't agree to become part of this story."

The editor's eyes went to Greg.

He raised both hands. "I think Jasper explained it pretty well."

She tapped her pen. "People are interested. Greg's been around forever. It's a local feel-good piece."

"Then let it feel good without claiming we signed an ownership deed," I said.

I heard how sharp I sounded and took a breath. "I'm ethically non-monogamous. I prefer polyamory. Greg knows, and we make our agreements privately. I don't want a headline that pretends he rescued me from every other relationship, or that I'm his reward for being lovable."

Greg looked at the floor and smiled at his shoes.

The editor read the caption again.

"You're right," she said. "I was trying to make a story out of a shortcut."

Greg cleared his throat. "Could you maybe mention the two teenagers who kept the sound board from falling over? They did the actual heroics."

"Not without asking them and their parents," the editor said.

"Good point."

We settled on a correction that named the music night, the performers who had agreed to be credited, and the money raised for instrument repairs. The next issue could carry the correct information. Online or not, the printed copies already out in town weren't going to vanish.

The editor called us back before we reached the door.

"One more question," she said. "If the caption was wrong, how should I describe your relationship when I cover the next concert?"

"By describing the concert," I said.

She looked down at her notebook, then back at me. "I suppose that sounds obvious."

"It does now."

Greg shifted beside me. He wasn't angry with her, exactly. He'd spent enough years hoping a newspaper would say his name to know how hard it was to resist an easy story.

"I don't want to pretend I'm single just because it's a shorter caption," he said. "But I don't want a headline about Jasper dating other people either."

I felt a rush of relief. We'd agreed to be honest about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory. That wasn't the same as inviting strangers into our calendar.

The editor nodded. "I can write that you performed together without labeling your lives."

"And please don't quote us discussing this," I added. "We're telling you what needs correcting, not giving a new interview."

She drew a line through her notes. I watched her do it. It wasn't a promise that nobody in Beach City would gossip. It was a small correction made by someone who could actually change a printed sentence.

Outside, the woman who'd asked about the free concert was waiting with a flyer. She wanted to know whether the music night had raised enough to repair the children's instruments.

"Not yet," Greg told her. "That's why we're having another one."

She asked for a contact so she could donate without buying a ticket. He gave her the community center's number, not ours. She left before either of us could turn her generosity into a story about ourselves.

I leaned against the van.

"That was exhausting."

"Yeah. Want me to drive somewhere with no reporters?"

"Anywhere with sandwiches."

"That's a beautiful vision of the future."

He reached out, paused, and waited for me to take his hand. I did. It wasn't the newspaper's version of a settled musician and a person who'd rescued him from wandering. It was a man with ink on his thumb and a person who still had other people to love, making a choice for one ordinary afternoon.

We could tell that story ourselves, or not tell it at all.

At the boardwalk lunch stand, the owner recognized Greg and asked whether he'd sign the menu board for a charity raffle.

"Maybe," Greg said. "Who's running it?"

She showed us the printed notice. The money was for instrument repairs at the community center, and Pilar had approved the event. Greg checked the date before agreeing. He didn't sign on behalf of me or the other musicians.

The owner offered our food for free.

"We can pay for sandwiches," he said, looking at the price list. "Could you send the raffle information to the center instead?"

She shrugged and handed over the bag. Her ordinary willingness to treat him like a customer seemed to make him relax more than being recognized had.

We sat near the van while the gulls patrolled the railing. One landed close enough to inspect my lunch with criminal intent.

"Don't even think about it," I warned.

Greg laughed. "You're negotiating with a bird."

"It's a boundary-setting exercise."

"You're getting really good at those."

I looked at him over the sandwich. I liked that he could joke about my anger without asking me to pretend it was gone.

"Do you wish the paper had said we were more conventional?" I asked.

"No. I wish it had asked before describing us. That's different."

I nodded. When we finished eating, we checked the fundraiser's date against his real schedule. He had time to participate if he wanted. I had commitments elsewhere, and neither of us had to turn the calendar into an accusation.

The gull stole a fallen crumb. I let it have that much. Greg said it was a diplomatic victory, and for once I agreed.

Greg glanced at me again as we turned toward the van.

"You okay?" he asked.

"Embarrassed. Annoyed. Weirdly hungry."

"That's a whole album."

"I'd buy it."

He nudged my shoulder with his. "You know, I liked how you said we chose each other."

"It was true."

"I got scared you were going to be mad at me for not stepping in sooner."

"You let me speak for myself. That wasn't abandoning me."

"Good. Because I was also busy thinking of twelve terrible jokes."

"Only twelve?"

"I've got standards."

We reached the van with our sandwich wrappers and drinks. Someone had taped a flyer to its window asking Greg to perform at a fundraiser he hadn't heard about. He read it, sighed, and wrote down the contact number. Being liked in a small town meant people assumed you could always say yes.

"You can decline," I said.

"Yeah. I know. I'm trying to remember that."

A gull stole the last scrap of bread from my wrapper. Greg laughed so hard he nearly lost his drink. I chased the bird a grand total of three steps before realizing the humiliation was complete.

Later, at the car wash office, we drafted a response to the fundraising committee and made a list of gigs he actually wanted to play. We kept separate calendars. He asked which dates affected us; I told him the ones that did. Neither of us needed a report on every other person I saw.

The correction came out the following week. It was small, under the community notices. It gave credit to the musicians and volunteers. It didn't put me on display.

Greg read it twice.

"They spelled my name right," he said. "That's new."

He reached for my hand. I let him take it.

"Can I kiss you?" he asked.

"Yes."

We kissed beside the van where anyone might have seen, and then I drew back laughing at his hair getting caught in the open window.

"You all right?" I asked.

"Romantically compromised," he said.

I shut the window. We kept the rest of the evening for ourselves, not because there was anything shameful to hide, but because some things were ours to choose.
